segments.narration: $26 per ounce: Track it, and profit.

Calculating your average cost per ounce of silver is crucial for understanding your investment returns and making informed decisions. At Fused Distribution, we stock a wide variety of silver bullion and coins, and we recommend careful tracking for all our clients. This guide will walk you through the process, step-by-step, ensuring you have a clear picture of your silver investment performance.

A consistent average cost per ounce provides a valuable reference point, especially when market fluctuations occur. It allows you to assess whether your investment strategy is working for you. The first step is to collect all your silver purchase records. This includes: Purchase Dates: Note the exact date of each transaction. Purchase Price: Record the price you paid per ounce for each purchase.

If you’re buying and selling frequently, consider using a dedicated investment tracking app. Once you’ve compiled your data, it’s time to calculate the total cost of your silver holdings. Sum up the “Price Per Ounce” column for all your purchases. Then, multiply that total by the “Ounces Purchased” column to get the total cost of your silver.

This will give you the total number of ounces of silver you currently hold. In our example, the total ounces held would be 10 + 5 + 2 = 17 ounces. Now, you can calculate your average cost per ounce. Divide the total cost of silver ($444) by the total number of ounces held (17). For more on this, see How To Build A Silver Inventory Spreadsheet.

Calculate the Sale Proceeds: Multiply the number of ounces sold by the sale price. Subtract the Sale Proceeds from the Total Cost: $444 (total cost) - $100 (sale proceeds) = $344 4. Add the New Ounces Held: 17 ounces (initial holdings) + 3 ounces (ounces sold) = 20 ounces 5. Calculate the New Average Cost: $344 / 20 = $17.20 per ounce.

Your new average cost per ounce is now $17.20. This reflects the impact of your sale on your overall investment. Your average cost per ounce is a key metric for assessing your profitability. It allows you to determine whether you’re making a profit or a loss on your silver investments. Compare your current average cost per ounce to the current spot price of silver.

For instance, if silver prices are generally rising, you can expect your average cost to increase over time. Conversely, if silver prices are falling, your average cost will likely decrease. This comparison can help you identify potential buying or selling opportunities. According to a recent report, silver prices have historically shown an upward trend. Not Tracking Purchases: Failing to record all your silver purchases is the most common mistake.

Relying Solely on Spot Price: While the spot price is important, your average cost per ounce provides a more accurate reflection of your individual investment performance.
